name: The Class for Representing a Point in the Euclidean Plane (Case 1)
description: Construct a class that represents a point in the Euclidean plane. The class should contain data that represents the point’s integer coordinates (x,y). The point's coordinates could be accessed or changed only through the getter and setter methods. The class should also include a method to translate the point, i.e., shift the point's location by the specified amount.
code:
#Step 1: Define the class
class Point1 :
    #Step 1.1: Declare the method to shift the location of the point by the given amount
    def translate(self, dx, dy) :
        self.__x += dx
        self.__y += dy
    #Step 1.2: Define the setter and getter methods for the x-coordinate of the point
    def set_x(self, new_x) :
        self.__x = new_x
    def get_x(self) :
        return self.__x
    #Step 1.3: Define the setter and getter methods for the y-coordinate of the point
    def set_y(self, new_y) :
        self.__y = new_y
    def get_y(self) :
        return self.__y
#Step 2: Test the class
p1 = Point1()
p1.set_x(7)
p1.set_y(2)
p1.translate(11, 6)
print("p1 coordinates: (" + str(p1.get_x()) + ", " + str(p1.get_y()) + ")")

comments.content: We define the class named Point1 to represent a point in the Euclidean plane.

This method shifts the coordinates of the point by a specific delta-x (dx) and delta-y (dy), which are passed as parameters. The first argument (named self) is passed in automatically by the interpreter when the method is invoked on an instance of the class. The second and third arguments are the amount that we want to shift the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the point, respectively.

Note that Python automatically fills the first argument in with the instance object that is the implied subject of the method call. Therefore, when this method is invoked on an instance of the class, only the last two parameters (dx and dy) must be passed to the method.

To shift the x-coordinate of the point, we need to add dx to the x-coordinate of that point.
self is the instance of the class and self.__x is the x-coordinate of the instance. We start the attribute name by two underscore (self.__x) to prevent accessing the attribute directly from outside of the class.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable dx) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of the instance attribute self.__x) and the result is stored in the instance attribute (self.__x). Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement self.__x = self.__x + dx.

To shift the y-coordinate of the point, we need to add dy to the y-coordinate of that point.
self is the instance of the class and self.__y is the y-coordinate of the instance. We start the attribute name by two underscore (self.__y) to prevent accessing the attribute directly from outside of the class.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable dy) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of the instance attribute self.__y) and the result is stored in the instance attribute (self.__y). Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement self.__y = self.__y + dy.

We create an instance of the class Point1 to demonstrate the creation and use of Point1 instances.
This statement creates a Point1 instance. The variable p1 holds a reference to a Point1 instance.
This statement invokes the method set_x of p1 to set its x-coordinate to 7. Note that p1 is the implied subject (instance) passed to self.
This statement invokes the method set_y of p1 to set its y-coordinate to 2. Note that p1 is the implied subject (instance) passed to self.

This statement invokes the method translate of p1. The translate method receives two parameters. The first parameter specifies how much we want to shift the x-coordinate of p1. The second parameter specifies how much we want to shift the y-coordinate of p1. Also, p1 is the implied subject (instance) passed to self.
Note that this method must be called after the set_x and set_y methods are called.

An error would occur if we call the translate method before we call the set_x and set_y methods. Because the class Point1 doesn't have a __init__() method that initialize the coordinates of the point. So by the time p1 is instantiated, the coordinates of p1 are not present. Therefore, We must first call the set_x and set_y methods to set the values of the coordinates.

This statement concatenates the content of the given strings and variables to print the coordinates of p1. To get p1's coordinates, we invoke the method get_x and get_y of p1. Note that we do not necessarily have to store the returned value from each of these methods in a variable. We could use the returned value of them directly in the print statement.

We concatenate the content of p1 coordinates with the other strings using the + operator. The coordinates of the point hold integer values and their values can be concatenated with strings only when they're explicitly converted to a string using the str function.
Note that the concatenating and printing are done in the same line. That is, we don't have to store the concatenated string to a new variable at first and then print it in the next line.
Note that the + operator creates a new string from the contents of its operands joined. This string will be printed by the print function and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
